claims.source: When fossil specimens are plotted a posteriori onto the tangent space identified by extant taxa, Oreopithecus (BAC 208; Figures 1n and 6a) falls on moderately positive scores for bgPC1 (where the distributions of hominids, cercopithecins, and platyrrhines overlap), while the two Australopithecus individuals (StW 573 and StW 578; Figures 1o,p and 6b–c) fall within the range of living great apes and humans (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the bgPCA results showing the position of Oreopithecus in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The two Australopithecus individuals (StW 573 and StW 578) fall within the range of living great apes and humans for bgPC1.
claims.source: When fossil specimens are plotted a posteriori onto the tangent space identified by extant taxa, Oreopithecus (BAC 208; Figures 1n and 6a) falls on moderately positive scores for bgPC1 (where the distributions of hominids, cercopithecins, and platyrrhines overlap), while the two Australopithecus individuals (StW 573 and StW 578; Figures 1o,p and 6b–c) fall within the range of living great apes and humans (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the bgPCA results showing the position of Australopithecus specimens in Figure 2.

claims.claim: StW 573 shows more evenly developed canals than StW 578 and BAC 208, which both display a smaller lateral canal.
claims.source: When the relative size of the SCs is taken into account, StW 573 shows more evenly developed canals than StW 578 and BAC 208, which both display a smaller lateral canal.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on morphological observations of the fossil specimens.

claims.claim: StW 573 falls on positive scores for bgPC2, close to the mean value for hominids and cercopithecoids.
claims.source: Their position along the bgPC2 axis reflects these differences, with StW 573 falling on positive scores (close to the mean value for hominids and cercopithecoids; Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b) and the other two specimens occupying moderately negative values (within the range of extant catarrhines and approaching that of platyrrhines; Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the bgPCA results showing the position of StW 573 in Figure 2a.

claims.claim: StW 578 and BAC 208 occupy moderately negative values for bgPC2, within the range of extant catarrhines and approaching that of platyrrhines.
claims.source: Their position along the bgPC2 axis reflects these differences, with StW 573 falling on positive scores (close to the mean value for hominids and cercopithecoids; Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b) and the other two specimens occupying moderately negative values (within the range of extant catarrhines and approaching that of platyrrhines; Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the bgPCA results showing the position of StW 578 and BAC 208 in Figure 2a.

claims.claim: Oreopithecus falls at the negative end of the extant anthropoid distribution for bgPC3 due to the acute angles between the planes identified by the anterior and lateral canals and that between the planes of the posterior and anterior canals.
claims.source: Due to the acute angles between the planes identified by the anterior and lateral canals and that between the planes of the posterior and anterior canals, Oreopithecus falls at the negative end of the extant anthropoid distribution for the bgPC3 (Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the bgPCA results and morphological observations presented in Figure 2b.

claims.claim: The two Australopithecus specimens occupy more intermediate values for bgPC3 because of the possession of a right angle between the planes of the anterior and posterior canals.
claims.source: On the other hand, the two Australopithecus specimens occupy more intermediate values because of the possession of a right angle between the planes of the aforementioned canals.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on morphological observations of the Australopithecus specimens.

claims.claim: StW 573 and 578 fall well within the great ape and human range when the bgPCs are considered at the same time.
claims.source: When the bgPCs are considered at the same time (Figure 2), the australopith specimens fall well within the great ape and human range.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the bgPCA results presented in Figure 2.

claims.claim: StW 573 is classified as hominids with p=0.678 based on posterior probabilities of group membership.
claims.source: This is further supported by their posterior probabilities of group membership based on the proximity of fossil specimen scores to groups centroids, with StW 573 and 578 being classified as hominids with p=0.678 and p=0.190, respectively (Table 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the posterior probability analysis results presented in Table 3.

claims.claim: StW 578 is classified as hominids with p=0.190 based on posterior probabilities of group membership.
claims.source: This is further supported by their posterior probabilities of group membership based on the proximity of fossil specimen scores to groups centroids, with StW 573 and 578 being classified as hominids with p=0.678 and p=0.190, respectively (Table 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the posterior probability analysis results presented in Table 3.

claims.claim: StW 573 falls close to Pan and Homo in the bgPCA morphospace.
claims.source: StW 573 falls close to Pan and Homo, whereas StW 578 occupies an intermediate position between humans and orangutans due to its stouter volumetric proportions.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the bgPCA results showing the position of StW 573 in the morphospace.

claims.claim: StW 578 occupies an intermediate position between humans and orangutans due to its stouter volumetric proportions.
claims.source: StW 573 falls close to Pan and Homo, whereas StW 578 occupies an intermediate position between humans and orangutans due to its stouter volumetric proportions.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the bgPCA results and morphological observations of StW 578.

claims.claim: When the posterior probabilities are computed using the centroids of the hominoid genera, StW 573 is classified as Pan as first option (p=0.368) and as Homo as second (p=0.264).
claims.source: When the posterior probabilities are computed using the centroids of the hominoid genera, StW 573 is classified as Pan as first option (p=0.368) and as Homo as second (p=0.264), while StW 578 is more clearly classified as Homo with p=0.727 (Table 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the posterior probability analysis results presented in Table 4.

claims.claim: StW 578 is more clearly classified as Homo with p=0.727 when posterior probabilities are computed using the centroids of the hominoid genera.
claims.source: When the posterior probabilities are computed using the centroids of the hominoid genera, StW 573 is classified as Pan as first option (p=0.368) and as Homo as second (p=0.264), while StW 578 is more clearly classified as Homo with p=0.727 (Table 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the posterior probability analysis results presented in Table 4.

claims.claim: Both australopith specimens show vestibular similarities with extant humans, but StW 573 displays a more plesiomorphic (chimpanzee-like) morphology.
claims.source: These results suggest that both australopith specimens show vestibular similarities with extant humans, but that StW 573 display a more plesiomorphic (chimpanzee-like) morphology.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the bgPCA and posterior probability results.

claims.claim: Oreopithecus shows a mosaic of vestibular features (Pan-like volumetric proportions, small lateral canal, and acute angles between the anterior and both the posterior and the lateral canals) that does not match the condition of any extant taxon.
claims.source: In turn, Oreopithecus shows a mosaic of vestibular features (Pan-like volumetric proportions, small lateral canal, and acute angles between the anterior and both the posterior and the lateral canals) that does not match the condition of any extant taxon (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on morphological observations and bgPCA results presented in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The posterior probabilities indicate that Oreopithecus shows closest similarities with cercopithecoids, followed by hominids and platyrrhines, although in all instances it falls outside the variability of the extant members of these groups (p<0.05).
claims.source: The posterior probabilities indicate closest similarities with cercopithecoids, followed by hominids and platyrrhines, although in all instances it falls outside the variability of the extant members of these groups (p<0.05; Table 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the posterior probability analysis results presented in Table 3.

claims.claim: When comparisons are restricted to hominoid genera, Oreopithecus appears more similar to humans than to any ape genus, but with a posterior probability that indicates significant differences with all of them (p<0.05).
claims.source: When comparisons are restricted to hominoid genera, Oreopithecus appears more similar to humans than to any ape genus, but again with a posterior probability that indicates significant differences with all of them (p<0.05; Table 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the posterior probability analysis results presented in Table 4.

claims.claim: The multivariate regression between shape (deformation fields) and size (log-transformed volume of the vestibule) shows a significant correlation (i.e., allometry) at p<0.001, but explains only a limited portion of the variance (R2 = 0.192).
claims.source: The multivariate regression between shape (deformation fields) and size (log-transformed volume of the vestibule) shows a significant correlation (i.e., allometry) at p<0.001, but nevertheless explains only a limited portion of the variance (R2 = 0.192).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the regression analysis results.

claims.claim: Bivariate regressions of the bgPCs against log-transformed cube root of vestibular volume reveal a significant correlation only for bgPC1 (R2 = 0.635, p<0.001).
claims.source: Bivariate regressions of the bgPCs against log-transformed cube root of vestibular volume reveal a significant correlation only for bgPC1 (R2 = 0.635, p<0.001, Table 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the regression analysis results presented in Table 2.

claims.claim: Allometry for bgPC1 is more marked in hominids than in other anthropoids.
claims.source: A visual inspection of the scatter of points (Figure 7a) suggests that allometry for bgPC1 is more marked in hominids. This is confirmed when separate regressions are performed for hominids (R2 = 0.480, p<0.001) and the rest of the sample (R2 = 0.058, p<0.01), with the former displaying also a higher slope (Table 5).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the regression analysis results presented in Figure 7a and Table 5.

claims.claim: When phylogeny is considered by means of PGLS regression, the correlation for bgPC1 vs. volume for the whole sample is still significant but explains much less variance (R2 = 0.261, p<0.01), becoming non-significant for hominids and the rest of the sample separately.
claims.source: When phylogeny is considered by means of PGLS regression (Table 5), the correlation for the whole sample is still significant but explains much less variance (R2 = 0.261, p<0.01), becoming non-significant for hominids and the rest of the sample separately.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the PGLS regression analysis results presented in Table 5.

claims.claim: Both Australopithecus and Oreopithecus overlap with the hominid scatter of points in the bgPC1 vs. volume plot, with the two australopith specimens falling above the hominid regression line, whereas BAC 208 falls slightly below.
claims.source: Both Australopithecus and Oreopithecus overlap with the hominid scatter of points, with the two australopith specimens falling above the hominid regression line, whereas BAC 208 falls slightly below (although well above that of non-hominid anthropoids).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the regression analysis results shown in Figure 7a.

claims.claim: The bivariate regression between the log-transformed cube root of the SC volume and SC length shows in all instances a significant correlation that nevertheless only explains a limited (ca. 20–30%) amount of variance.
claims.source: The bivariate regression between the log-transformed cube root of the SC volume and SC length shows in all instances a significant correlation that nevertheless only explains a limited (ca. 20–30%) amount of variance (Table 5, Figure 7b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the regression analysis results presented in Table 5 and Figure 7b.

claims.claim: Isometry cannot be rejected for anthropoids as a whole in the relationship between SC volume and length, but a negatively allometric relationship emerges when hominids and other taxa are analyzed separately.
claims.source: Isometry cannot be rejected for anthropoids as a whole, but a negatively allometric relationship emerges (revealing that length increases faster than volume) when hominids and other taxa are analyzed separately (Table 5).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the regression analysis results presented in Table 5.

claims.claim: There is an allometric grade shift between hominids and the remaining anthropoid taxa in the relationship between SC volume and length, indicating that hominids possess more voluminous (i.e., stouter) canals than other anthropoids at equal lengths.
claims.source: The bivariate plot (Figure 7b) shows an allometric grade shift between hominids and the remaining anthropoid taxa, which is confirmed by ANCOVA results—indicating no significant differences (F = 0.705, p=0.403) between the allometric slopes but significantly different intercepts (F = 263.26, p<0.001) between the two groups. This indicates that hominids possess more voluminous (i.e., stouter) canals than other anthropoids at equal lengths, with only minimal overlap.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the regression analysis and ANCOVA results presented in Figure 7b.

claims.claim: All the fossil specimens display hominid-like volumetric proportions in the SC volume vs. length relationship.
claims.source: All the fossil specimens display hominid-like volumetric proportions (Figure 7b): StW 573 and 578 fall slightly above the hominid regression line, whereas BAC 208, due to its slenderer semicircular canals, falls below (although much closer than to the non-hominid regression line).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the regression analysis results shown in Figure 7b.

claims.claim: The principal components resulting from the vestibular shape GM analyses show a preexisting group structure similar to that showed by bgPCA for both extant and fossil taxa.
claims.source: Prior to computing the bgPCA, we explored the principal components resulting from the vestibular shape GM analyses to investigate the presence of a preexisting group structure, which was found to be similar to that showed by bgPCA for both extant and fossil taxa (Figure 8).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the PCA results presented in Figure 8.

claims.claim: The confusion matrix resulting from the HCA shows that most individuals are correctly identified in the corresponding groups.
claims.source: The confusion matrix resulting from the HCA shows that most individuals are correctly identified in the corresponding groups (Table 6).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the HCA results presented in Table 6.

claims.claim: In the deformation-based analyses, hylobatids show a low percentage of classification (24% of the individuals), mostly due to the great similarity in the volumetric proportions and surface shape of the vestibule between this group and cercopithecoids.
claims.source: Only in the deformation-based analyses hylobatids show a low percentage of classification (24% of the individuals), mostly due to the great similarity in the volumetric proportions and surface shape of the vestibule between this group and cercopithecoids.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the HCA results and morphological observations.

claims.claim: The deformation-based and landmark-based analyses yielded similar group separation, as shown by the components resulting from the bgPCA.
claims.source: We thus compared our deformation-based results with those obtained from a configuration of 3D semilandmarks commonly used to investigate the vestibular shape (Gunz et al., 2012). Both analyses, based on the full primate sample, yielded a similar group separation (compare Figure 2 with Figure 9), as shown by the components resulting from the bgPCA.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparing the bgPCA results in Figure 2 and Figure 9.

claims.claim: Shape variation in the analyzed sample, as captured by landmark-based 3DGM, accounts for a strong phylogenetic signal (Kmult = 0.973, p<0.001).
claims.source: Shape variation in the analyzed sample, as captured by landmark-based 3DGM, accounts for a strong phylogenetic signal (Kmult = 0.973, p<0.001), and this also holds for the first three bgPCs separately (see below).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the phylogenetic signal analysis results for the landmark-based approach.

claims.claim: In the landmark-based approach, hylobatids largely overlap with great apes in both bgPC1 and bgPC2, but can be distinguished from them (and other anthropoids) to a large extent based on bgPC3.
claims.source: In the landmark-based approach, hylobatids largely overlap with great apes in both bgPC1 (occupying an intermediate position) and bgPC2 (Figure 9a), but can be distinguished from them (and other anthropoids) to a large extent based on bgPC3 (Figure 9b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the landmark-based bgPCA results presented in Figure 9.

claims.claim: In the landmark-based analysis, bgPC1 (53.3% of total variance) embeds a strong phylogenetic signal (λ = 1 and K = 1.26).
claims.source: Shape differences along bgPC1 (53.3% of total variance) in the landmark-based approach embed a strong phylogenetic signal (λ = 1 and K = 1.26; Table 7).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the phylogenetic signal analysis results presented in Table 7.

claims.claim: In the landmark-based analysis, bgPC1 correlates with the insertion of the lateral canal on the vestibule, the size and shape of the posterior canal, and the roundness of the SCs.
claims.source: This component correlates with the insertion of the lateral canal on the vestibule, the size and shape of the posterior canal, and the roundness of the SCs.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the interpretation of the landmark-based bgPCA results.

claims.claim: In the landmark-based analysis, great apes and humans fall on negative values for bgPC1 as they are characterized by smaller canals compared to the size of the vestibular recesses and less rounded SCs (particularly the anterior one, which is vertically compressed).
claims.source: Great apes and humans fall on negative values for the first axis (Figure 9c), as they are characterized by smaller canals compared to the size of the vestibular recesses and less rounded SCs (particularly the anterior one, which is vertically compressed).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the landmark-based bgPCA results presented in Figure 9c.

claims.claim: In the landmark-based analysis, hylobatids stand on intermediate scores for bgPC1 that largely overlap with the hominid range due to a combination of long SCs, a vertically compressed anterior canal, and well separated lateral and posterior canals.
claims.source: Hylobatids stand on intermediate scores that largely overlap with the hominid range (Figure 9) due to a combination of long SCs, a vertically compressed anterior canal, and well separated lateral and posterior canals (since posterior canal is posteriorly displaced and the lateral canal inserts anteriorly in the vestibule).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the landmark-based bgPCA results presented in Figure 9.

claims.claim: In the landmark-based analysis, Old world monkeys tend to be located on positive values of bgPC1 and display a protruding lateral canal that intersects the plane defined by the posterior canal.
claims.source: In contrast, Old world monkeys tend to be located on positive values of bgPC1 and display a protruding lateral canal that intersects the plane defined by the posterior canal.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the landmark-based bgPCA results.

claims.claim: In the landmark-based analysis, bgPC2 (29.3% of variance) separates platyrrhines—especially Ateles—from other anthropoids due to the more reduced lateral canal in the former.
claims.source: bgPC2 (29.3% of variance) separates platyrrhines—especially Ateles found in the most negative scores (Figure 1i)—from other anthropoids due to the more reduced lateral canal in the former, which is inversely proportional to anterior canal development and vertical elongation (Figure 9d).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the landmark-based bgPCA results presented in Figure 9d.

claims.claim: In the landmark-based analysis, the phylogenetic signal displayed by bgPC2 is slightly reduced as compared to bgPC1, but still significant and very high (λ = 0.9 and K = 1.08).
claims.source: The identified phylogenetic signal displayed by bgPC2 is slightly reduced as compared to bgPC1, but still significant and very high (λ = 0.9 and K = 1.08;).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the phylogenetic signal analysis results for the landmark-based approach.

claims.claim: In the landmark-based analysis, bgPC3 (17.4% of variance) is driven by both trajectory and size of the SCs, especially of the posterior one, and displays less phylogenetic signal than bgPC1 and bgPC2 (λ = 0.93 and K = 0.53).
claims.source: The bgPC3 (17.4% of variance) is driven by both trajectory and size of the SCs, especially of the posterior one (Figure 9e), and displays less phylogenetic signal than bgPC1 and bgPC2 (λ = 0.93 and K = 0.53, Table 7).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the landmark-based bgPCA results and phylogenetic signal analysis presented in Figure 9e and Table 7.

claims.claim: In the landmark-based analysis, the two Australopithecus specimens overlap with the range of great apes and humans for all the bgPCs.
claims.source: When plotted onto the tangent space of extant taxa, the two Australopithecus specimens overlap with the range of great apes and humans for all the bgPCs (Figure 9, Figure 9—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the landmark-based bgPCA results presented in Figure 9.

claims.claim: In the landmark-based analysis, StW 578 overlaps with extant human variation in both bgPC1 and bgPC2, whereas StW 573 overlaps instead with chimpanzees and bonobos.
claims.source: The two specimens can be distinguished from one another by means of bgPC2 (Figure 9a), with StW 573 falling on positive values and StW 578 occupying negative ones. This is explained by the smaller lateral canal relative to the vertical SCs in StW 578, which therefore overlaps with extant human variation in both bgPC1 and bgPC2, whereas StW 573 overlaps instead with chimpanzees and bonobos (Figure 9a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the landmark-based bgPCA results presented in Figure 9a.

claims.claim: In the landmark-based analysis, Oreopithecus displays more positive values than hominoids for bgPC1 and falls well within the range of non-hominoid anthropoids.
claims.source: In turn, along bgPC1 Oreopithecus displays more positive values than hominoids and falls well within the range of non-hominoid anthropoids (it only slightly overlaps with the positive end of the hominoid distribution; Figure 9) due to its more coplanar lateral canal that almost intersects the plane defined by the posterior canal.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the landmark-based bgPCA results presented in Figure 9.

claims.claim: The two 3DGM techniques used in this paper generally yielded similar results except for hylobatids and Oreopithecus (along bgPC1 alone).
claims.source: Overall, the two 3DGM techniques used in this paper generally yielded similar results except for hylobatids and Oreopithecus (along bgPC1 alone).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on comparing the results of the deformation-based and landmark-based analyses.

claims.claim: The differences between the two 3DGM techniques are attributable to differences in the underlying methodological assumptions of each method when computing shape variation.
claims.source: This is attributable to differences in the underlying methodological assumptions of each method when computing shape variation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the methodological reasons for the observed differences.

claims.claim: The 3DGM landmark protocol measures the spatial trajectory of SCs based on their midline skeleton and hence does not capture differences in volumetric proportions.
claims.source: In particular, our 3DGM landmark protocol measures the spatial trajectory of SCs based on their midline skeleton (Gunz et al., 2012) and hence it does not capture differences in volumetric proportions.
claims.evidence: The claim cites Gunz et al., 2012 for the landmark protocol and explains its limitations.

claims.claim: By comparing surfaces as a whole, the deformation analysis is particularly sensitive to volumetric differences.
claims.source: In contrast, by comparing surfaces as a whole (Durrleman et al., 2012b; Durrleman et al., 2012a), the deformation analysis is particularly sensitive to volumetric differences.
claims.evidence: The claim cites Durrleman et al., 2012b and Durrleman et al., 2012a for the deformation method and explains its advantages.

claims.claim: The amount of identified phylogenetic signal is very similar for both deformation-based and landmark-based techniques, affecting the entire variance.
claims.source: In addition, the amount of identified phylogenetic signal is very similar for both techniques, affecting the entire variance.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on comparing the phylogenetic signal results for both techniques.

claims.claim: The separation found between the groups in the bgPCA of this study already exists in the shape data and is not a spurious effect produced by the bgPCA method itself.
claims.source: Together with the results of the HCA, we confidently show that the separation found between the groups in the bgPCA of this study already exists in the shape data and that is not a spurious effect produced by the bgPCA method itself.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the HCA and PCA results.

claims.claim: The phylomorphospace approach applied to vestibular shape variation in hominoids infers different branch lengths for hominids and hylobatids from the ancestral morphology estimated for crown hominoids.
claims.source: The phylomorphospace approach applied to vestibular shape variation in hominoids infers different branch lengths for hominids and hylobatids from the ancestral morphology estimated for crown hominoids, which falls much closer to great apes and humans than to hylobatids for both bgPC1 and bgPC3 (Figure 10).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the phylomorphospace analysis results presented in Figure 10.

claims.claim: The crown hominoid LCA vestibular morphology would be characterized by equally developed and slightly inflated SCs, a fairly vertically compressed anterior canal, and by the slender portion of the lateral canal connecting more anteromedially with the vestibule.
claims.source: According to our reconstructions based on the extant taxa (Figure 10), the crown hominoid LCA vestibular morphology (Figure 11a) would be characterized by equally developed and slightly inflated SCs, a fairly vertically compressed anterior canal, and by the slender portion of the lateral canal connecting more anteromedially with the vestibule.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the ancestral state reconstruction results presented in Figures 10 and 11a.

claims.claim: The estimated morphology for the LCA of hylobatids resembles to some extent that of the crown hominoid LCA, combined with more monkey-like features and others exclusive to hylobatids.
claims.source: The estimated morphology for the LCA of hylobatids (Figure 11b) resembles to some extent that of the crown hominoid LCA (slightly vertically compressed anterior canal and lack of intersection between the lateral and posterior canals), combined with more monkey-like features (markedly slender canals with inflated ampullae), and others exclusive to hylobatids (an obtuse angle between a slightly anteriorly protruding anterior canal and a small posterior canal relative to the others).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the ancestral state reconstruction results presented in Figure 11b.

claims.claim: Hylobatid genera are generally less diverging from one other than great apes and humans.
claims.source: Hylobatid genera are generally less diverging from one other than great apes and humans.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the phylomorphospace analysis.

claims.claim: Hoolock apparently displays the most primitive morphology among hylobatids.
claims.source: Hoolock (Figures 1f, 3f, 4f and 5f) apparently displays the most primitive morphology among hylobatids (with equally developed, rounded, almost orthogonal canals, and less anteriorly protruding anterior canal), while Hylobates (Figures 1h, 3h, 4h and 5h) and, to a lesser extent, Symphalangus (Figures 1g, 3g, 4g and 5g) show the slenderest SCs and an extremely anteriorly protruding anterior canal (as noted by Le Maître et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on morphological observations and ancestral state reconstruction results, with a citation to Le Maître et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Hylobates and, to a lesser extent, Symphalangus show the slenderest SCs and an extremely anteriorly protruding anterior canal.
claims.source: Hoolock (Figures 1f, 3f, 4f and 5f) apparently displays the most primitive morphology among hylobatids (with equally developed, rounded, almost orthogonal canals, and less anteriorly protruding anterior canal), while Hylobates (Figures 1h, 3h, 4h and 5h) and, to a lesser extent, Symphalangus (Figures 1g, 3g, 4g and 5g) show the slenderest SCs and an extremely anteriorly protruding anterior canal (as noted by Le Maître et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on morphological observations, with a citation to Le Maître et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The reconstructed morphologies for LCAs of crown hominids and, to a lesser extent, crown hominines and the Pan-Homo clade are not very far from the crown hominoid ancestral condition for any of the first three bgPCs.
claims.source: The reconstructed morphologies for LCAs of crown hominids (Figure 11c) and, to a lesser extent, crown hominines (Figure 11d) and the Pan-Homo clade (Figure 11e) are not very far from the crown hominoid ancestral condition (Figure 11a) for any of the first three bgPCs.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the ancestral state reconstruction results presented in Figure 11.

claims.claim: The crown hominid LCA is characterized by a lateral insertion of the slender portion of the lateral canal on the vestibule, a moderate medioventral displacement of the posterior canal, and an increased vertical compression of the anterior canal, in combination with thick and bulgy canals and well-developed vestibular recesses.
claims.source: The crown hominid LCA is characterized by a lateral insertion of the slender portion of the lateral canal on the vestibule, a moderate medioventral displacement of the posterior canal, and an increased vertical compression of the anterior canal, in combination with thick and bulgy canals and well-developed vestibular recesses.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the ancestral state reconstruction results.

claims.claim: The hominine and Pan-Homo clade LCAs possess stouter canals and are very similar to one another, distinguished only by the size of the lateral and anterior canals.
claims.source: The hominine and Pan-Homo clade LCAs possess stouter canals and are very similar to one another, distinguished only by the size of the lateral and anterior canals.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the ancestral state reconstruction results.

claims.claim: The LCA of the Pan-Homo clade shows a larger and less vertically compressed anterior canal, and a smaller lateral one, which also connects more anteriorly with the vestibule.
claims.source: The LCA of the Pan-Homo clade shows a larger and less vertically compressed anterior canal, and a smaller lateral one, which also connects more anteriorly with the vestibule.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the ancestral state reconstruction results.

claims.claim: The hominin (Australopithecus-Homo) LCA is closer to Homo, being characterized by the stoutest volumetric proportions, with larger vertical canals relative to the Pan-Homo clade LCA, yet smaller than those found in humans.
claims.source: The hominin (Australopithecus-Homo) LCA (Figure 11f) is closer to Homo, being characterized by the stoutest volumetric proportions, with larger vertical canals relative to the Pan-Homo clade LCA, yet smaller than those found in humans.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the ancestral state reconstruction results presented in Figure 11f.

claims.claim: The anterior canal of the hominin LCA is more vertically compressed than in Homo, rather resembling the morphology of Pan, while the posterior canal is rounded, thus being intermediate between the human (laterally projecting) and the chimpanzee (laterally compressed) morphology.

claims.source: Finally, Gorilla and Homo (Figures 1a, 3d, 4d and 5d) are derived in opposite directions along bgPC2 (Figure 10a), as the former exhibits increased lateral canal radius with a flattened cross-section, while humans retain quite rounded canals shape and cross-section, and show a reduction of the lateral canal, as opposed to more developed anterior and posterior canals.

claims.claim: Australopithecus is closer to humans than to any great ape, due to the possession of large vertical canals and stout volumetric proportions.
claims.source: Australopithecus is closer to humans than to any great ape, due to the possession of large vertical canals and stout volumetric proportions, being closest to the LCA of the Australopithecus-Homo clade and only slightly more derived in the same direction as Pongo due to the stouter canals (Figure 10).

claims.claim: Oreopithecus appears more plesiomorphic than humans and extant great apes in volumetric proportions, resembling those found in the LCA of crown hominoids.

claims.claim: Oreopithecus is clearly distinct from hylobatids in both SC stoutness and shape, being most clearly distinguished from gibbons and siamangs based on the acute angles defined the anterior canal with both the posterior and lateral canals.

claims.claim: Oreopithecus is also derived in terms of SC size (with the vertical canals much larger than the lateral one), similarly to humans albeit to a greater extent, and opposite to gorillas, due to the remarkably smaller lateral canal.
claims.source: Oreopithecus is also derived in terms of SC size (with the vertical canals much larger than the lateral one), similarly to humans albeit to a greater extent, and opposite to gorillas, due to the remarkably smaller lateral canal.

claims.claim: Main anthropoid groups can be distinguished based on vestibular shape variation.
claims.source: Our results indicate that main anthropoid groups can be distinguished based on vestibular shape variation, and that there are important differences not only between hylobatids, great apes, and humans, but also among extant great ape genera.

claims.claim: There are important differences not only between hylobatids, great apes, and humans, but also among extant great ape genera in vestibular morphology.
claims.source: Our results indicate that main anthropoid groups can be distinguished based on vestibular shape variation, and that there are important differences not only between hylobatids, great apes, and humans, but also among extant great ape genera.

claims.claim: A significant phylogenetic signal is found to affect the entire variance of the anthropoid sample.
claims.source: A significant phylogenetic signal is found to affect the entire variance of the anthropoid sample.

claims.claim: The shape of the SCs is overall informative from a phylogenetic viewpoint.
claims.source: Thus, the shape of the SCs is overall informative from a phylogenetic viewpoint—as hypothesized for strepsirrhine primates (Lebrun et al., 2010) and carnivorans (Schwab et al., 2019), but in contrast to previous results for hominoids (Le Maître et al., 2017) and some other mammals (Grohé et al., 2016; Costeur et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the phylogenetic signal analysis results, with citations to supporting and contrasting studies.

claims.claim: Several potential hominoid synapomorphies can be identified based on the analysis of the shape of the vestibular apparatus, including a posteromedially displaced posterior canal and a straight segment between the lateral-most point of the lateral canal and its anteromedially situated insertion on the vestibule.
claims.source: Based on the analysis of the shape of the vestibular apparatus, we identify several potential hominoid synapomorphies (Table 8; Figure 12a–g), including among others a posteromedially displaced posterior canal and a straight segment between the lateral-most point of the lateral canal and its anteromedially situated insertion on the vestibule.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the morphological analysis and ancestral state reconstructions, with reference to Table 8 and Figure 12.

claims.claim: The anteromedially located lateral canal in hominoids would imply an increased sensitivity for angular accelerations occurring along the coronal plane, which has been correlated with orthogrady in extant hominoids.
claims.source: This would imply an increased sensitivity for angular accelerations occurring along the coronal plane, which has been correlated with orthogrady in extant hominoids (Le Maître et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference about the functional implications of the morphology, with a citation to Le Maître et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The most evident character shared by extant apes and humans is the vertical compression of the anterior canal.
claims.source: The most evident character shared by extant apes and humans (even if somewhat variable in the latter and in Hoolock), and further displayed by the extinct genera analyzed here, is the vertical compression of the anterior canal (Figure 12a), as noted for great apes only in a previous analysis (Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on morphological observations, with a citation to Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998.

claims.claim: The hominoid morphology of the anterior canal might be related to the absence of the subarcuate fossa in great apes and siamangs.
claims.source: Since the subarcuate fossa arguably constrains the shape of the anterior canal (Jeffery et al., 2008), the hominoid morphology might be related to the absence of the fossa in great apes and siamangs (Moyà-Solà and Köhler, 1993; Gannon et al., 1988; Spoor and Leakey, 1996).
claims.evidence: The claim is a hypothesis about the relationship between the subarcuate fossa and anterior canal morphology, with citations to supporting studies.

claims.claim: The combination of a well-developed fossa and marked vertical compression of the anterior SC found in Hylobates argues against the hypothesis that the hominoid morphology is related to the absence of the subarcuate fossa.
claims.source: However, the combination of a well-developed fossa and marked vertical compression of the anterior SC found in Hylobates argues against this hypothesis.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on morphological observations of Hylobates.

claims.claim: The cercopithecoid morphology, characterized by a rounded anterior SC even in the largest terrestrial genera, further rejects the hypothesis that the hominoid morphology is related to the absence of the subarcuate fossa.
claims.source: The latter is further rejected by the cercopithecoid morphology, characterized by a rounded anterior SC even in the largest terrestrial genera (Papio, Theropithecus, and Mandrillus), which unlike other cercopithecoids display a much reduced (or even absent) subarcuate fossa (Gannon et al., 1988; Spoor and Leakey, 1996).
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on morphological observations of cercopithecoids, with citations to supporting studies.

claims.claim: All hominoids display the anterior canal projected anterosuperiorly to some extent as a result of vertical compression.
claims.source: As a result of vertical compression, all hominoids display the anterior canal projected anterosuperiorly to some extent (less accentuated in Homo and Hoolock).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on morphological observations.

claims.claim: The anterior projection of the anterior canal in Hylobates has been interpreted as a hylobatid synapomorphy.
claims.source: Such a projection of the anterior canal in Hylobates has been interpreted as a hylobatid synapomorphy (Le Maître et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim cites Le Maître et al., 2017 for this interpretation.

claims.claim: The results of this study raise doubts about the view that the anterior projection of the anterior canal is a hylobatid synapomorphy and indicate instead that it is variable within both hylobatids and hominids.
claims.source: Our results raise doubts about the latter view and indicate instead that the anterior projection of this canal is variable within both hylobatids and hominids, and that the LCA of crown hylobatids might have not shown the patent elongation of the anterior canal that is found in Hylobates and Symphalangus.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the morphological analysis and ancestral state reconstructions.

claims.claim: Two potential synapomorphies for hylobatids are an obtuse angle between the planes defined by the anterior and posterior canals, and a posteriorly-inclined posterior canal, which is smaller relative to the anterior and lateral ones.
claims.source: On the other hand, here we identify two potential synapomorphies for hylobatids (Table 8; Figure 12h,i): an obtuse angle between the planes defined by the anterior and posterior canals, and a posteriorly-inclined posterior canal, which is smaller relative to the anterior and lateral ones.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the morphological analysis and ancestral state reconstructions, with reference to Table 8 and Figure 12.

claims.claim: Hominids differ from other anthropoids, including hylobatids, by derived volumetric proportions of the SCs (stouter canals relative to their length, or shorter canals relative to their volume) even when size-scaling considerations are taken into account.
claims.source: In particular, hominids differ from other anthropoids, including hylobatids, by derived volumetric proportions of the SCs (stouter canals relative to their length, or shorter canals relative to their volume) even when size-scaling considerations are taken into account, as well as by the possession of more extensive vestibular recess for a similar size of the SCs (Table 8; Figure 12j,k), as reflected in bgPC1.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the morphological analysis and allometry results, with reference to Table 8 and Figure 12.

claims.claim: Hominids possess more extensive vestibular recess for a similar size of the SCs compared to other anthropoids.
claims.source: In particular, hominids differ from other anthropoids, including hylobatids, by derived volumetric proportions of the SCs (stouter canals relative to their length, or shorter canals relative to their volume) even when size-scaling considerations are taken into account, as well as by the possession of more extensive vestibular recess for a similar size of the SCs (Table 8; Figure 12j,k), as reflected in bgPC1.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the morphological analysis, with reference to Table 8 and Figure 12.

claims.claim: Cercopithecoids and hylobatids completely overlap due to the possession of slender SCs, while hominids differ by their swollen and relatively shorter SCs.
claims.source: In particular, cercopithecoids and hylobatids completely overlap due to the possession of slender SCs, while hominids as a whole (even if more markedly orangutans) differ by their swollen and relatively shorter SCs (with only few cercopithecins falling within the hominid range).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the morphological analysis and bgPCA results.

claims.claim: The slender SCs of hylobatids and cercopithecoids might be related to the fact that they are swift moving animals that make fast and large head movements, thus requiring a limited duct sensitivity to avoid overstimulation and a quick response to angular displacement.
claims.source: This might be related to the fact that hylobatids and cercopithecoids, unlike great apes, are swift moving animals that make fast and large head movements, thus requiring a limited duct sensitivity to avoid overstimulation and a quick response to angular displacement (Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998).
claims.evidence: The claim is a hypothesis about the functional implications of the morphology, with a citation to Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998.

claims.claim: Biophysical models suggest that the length of the membranous ducts is inversely proportional to their sensitivity and that a larger lumen of the ducts correlates with a reduced steadiness of the response to an external angular stimulus.
claims.source: This hypothesis is supported by biophysical models suggesting that the length of the membranous ducts is inversely proportional to their sensitivity and that a larger lumen of the ducts correlates with a reduced steadiness of the response to an external angular stimulus (i.e., the abrupt change of the position and/or posture) (Muller, 1994; Rabbitt et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: The claim cites Muller, 1994 and Rabbitt et al., 2004 for the biophysical models.

claims.claim: Species with shorter and thicker ducts (such as hominids) require more time to perceive and react to sudden head displacements, while being more sensitive to fine movements.
claims.source: Therefore, species with shorter and thicker ducts (such as hominids) require more time to perceive and react to sudden head displacements, while being more sensitive to fine movements.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the biophysical models and morphological observations.

claims.claim: Caution must be used when inferring the lumen of the ducts from that of the bony canals, as the amount of the SC cross-section occupied by perilymphatic space is variable depending on the species.
claims.source: Nevertheless, caution must be used when inferring the lumen of the ducts from that of the bony canals, as the amount of the SC cross-section occupied by perilymphatic space is variable depending on the species (Ramprashad et al., 1984; Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998).
claims.evidence: The claim cites Ramprashad et al., 1984 and Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998 for the variability in perilymphatic space.

claims.claim: There are marked differences among hominid genera in vestibular morphology, mainly relating to the relative size among the SCs.
claims.source: Superimposed on the aforementioned hominoid and hominid synapomorphies (Table 8; Figure 12), there are also marked differences among hominid genera. Such differences mainly relate the relative size among the SCs (which varies particularly along bgPC2 and bgPC3), while hylobatid genera are less diverse in this regard.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the bgPCA results.

claims.claim: Hylobatid genera are less diverse in vestibular morphology than hominid genera.
claims.source: Superimposed on the aforementioned hominoid and hominid synapomorphies (Table 8; Figure 12), there are also marked differences among hominid genera. Such differences mainly relate the relative size among the SCs (which varies particularly along bgPC2 and bgPC3), while hylobatid genera are less diverse in this regard.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the bgPCA results.

claims.claim: Chimpanzees and bonobos are characterized by equally developed SCs and a moderately short CC.
claims.source: Chimpanzees and bonobos are characterized by equally developed SCs and a moderately short CC.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on morphological observations.

claims.claim: Orangutans possess evenly proportioned SCs and can be distinguished from Pan by a shorter CC, more inflated canals, and a greater vertical compression of the anterior SC.
claims.source: Similarly, orangutans possess evenly proportioned SCs and can be distinguished from Pan by a shorter CC, more inflated canals, and a greater vertical compression of the anterior SC.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on morphological observations.

claims.claim: Gorillas display the largest intrageneric variability in the studied sample, especially with regard to SCs slenderness, coupled with some other distinctive traits (obtuse angle of the CC apex, and longer lateral SC and CC).
claims.source: Gorillas display the largest intrageneric variability in the studied sample, especially with regard to SCs slenderness, coupled with some other distinctive traits (obtuse angle of the CC apex, and longer lateral SC and CC).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on morphological observations.

claims.claim: Humans differ from apes in the enlarged vertical canals, a laterally protruding and inferiorly displaced posterior canal, and a moderately smaller lateral canal.
claims.source: Humans differ from apes in the enlarged vertical canals, a laterally protruding and inferiorly displaced posterior canal, and a moderately smaller lateral canal.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on morphological observations.

claims.claim: Relatively enlarged vertical canals are also found in Theropithecus.
claims.source: Relatively enlarged vertical canals are also found in Theropithecus.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on morphological observations.

claims.claim: The human morphology of enlarged vertical canals has been linked to bipedalism.
claims.source: The human morphology has been linked to bipedalism (Spoor et al., 1994; Spoor et al., 2003), as accelerations during bipedal walking mainly occur along the vertical axis, so that the broadly similar morphology of Theropithecus might be related to the bipedal shuffling characteristic of this genus during foraging, causing them spend an extremely large amount of time with an erect trunk posture (Wrangham, 1980).
claims.evidence: The claim cites Spoor et al., 1994 and Spoor et al., 2003 for the link to bipedalism.

claims.claim: The broadly similar morphology of Theropithecus might be related to the bipedal shuffling characteristic of this genus during foraging, causing them spend an extremely large amount of time with an erect trunk posture.
claims.source: The human morphology has been linked to bipedalism (Spoor et al., 1994; Spoor et al., 2003), as accelerations during bipedal walking mainly occur along the vertical axis, so that the broadly similar morphology of Theropithecus might be related to the bipedal shuffling characteristic of this genus during foraging, causing them spend an extremely large amount of time with an erect trunk posture (Wrangham, 1980).
claims.evidence: The claim is a hypothesis about the functional implications of the morphology, with a citation to Wrangham, 1980.

claims.claim: Vestibular variation bears strong phylogenetic signal and has potential for reconstructing the evolutionary history of hominoids.
claims.source: Irrespective of the functional implications of the variation in vestibular morphology among anthropoids, our analyses show that this variation bears strong phylogenetic signal and, hence, has potential for reconstructing the evolutionary history of the group—particularly hominoids, which in spite of their extant decimated diversity are more variable in this regard (particularly when size differences among the SCs are considered) (Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998; Le Maître et al., 2017) than the taxonomically more diverse cercopithecoids.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the phylogenetic signal analysis results, with citations to Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998 and Le Maître et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Hominoids are more variable in vestibular morphology than the taxonomically more diverse cercopithecoids.
claims.source: Irrespective of the functional implications of the variation in vestibular morphology among anthropoids, our analyses show that this variation bears strong phylogenetic signal and, hence, has potential for reconstructing the evolutionary history of the group—particularly hominoids, which in spite of their extant decimated diversity are more variable in this regard (particularly when size differences among the SCs are considered) (Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998; Le Maître et al., 2017) than the taxonomically more diverse cercopithecoids.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the morphological analysis results, with citations to Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998 and Le Maître et al., 2017.

claims.claim: To the extent that vestibular morphology appears to be linked to positional behavior, the higher variation of vestibular morphology displayed by hominoids compared to cercopithecoids agrees with the more diverse and varied locomotor repertoires of the former.
claims.source: Therefore, to the extent that vestibular morphology appears to be linked to positional behavior (Spoor et al., 1994; Spoor et al., 2007; Walker et al., 2008; Silcox et al., 2009; Ryan et al., 2012; Le Maître et al., 2017), the higher variation of vestibular morphology displayed by hominoids compared to cercopithecoids agrees with the more diverse and varied locomotor repertoires of the former.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference about the relationship between vestibular morphology and locomotor diversity, with citations to supporting studies.

claims.claim: Cercopithecoids as a whole are largely pronograde terrestrial quadrupeds that mostly differ in the degree of arboreality vs. terrestriality.
claims.source: This is because cercopithecoids as a whole are largely pronograde terrestrial quadrupeds that mostly differ in the degree of arboreality vs. terrestriality (Fleagle, 2013; Gosselin-Ildari, 2013), while crown hominoids are characterized by a derived and versatile orthograde body plan and associated adaptations throughout the body that enable very different and very specialized antipronograde behaviors—vertical climbing (all apes), ricochetal brachiation (hylobatids), arboreal quadrumanous suspension and clambering (orangutans), below-branch arm-swinging as well as semiterrestrial knuckle-walking (African apes), and terrestrial bipedalism (humans) (Hunt, 1991; Thorpe and Crompton, 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is a statement about cercopithecoid locomotion, with citations to Fleagle, 2013 and Gosselin-Ildari, 2013.

claims.claim: Crown hominoids are characterized by a derived and versatile orthograde body plan and associated adaptations throughout the body that enable very different and very specialized antipronograde behaviors.
claims.source: This is because cercopithecoids as a whole are largely pronograde terrestrial quadrupeds that mostly differ in the degree of arboreality vs. terrestriality (Fleagle, 2013; Gosselin-Ildari, 2013), while crown hominoids are characterized by a derived and versatile orthograde body plan and associated adaptations throughout the body that enable very different and very specialized antipronograde behaviors—vertical climbing (all apes), ricochetal brachiation (hylobatids), arboreal quadrumanous suspension and clambering (orangutans), below-branch arm-swinging as well as semiterrestrial knuckle-walking (African apes), and terrestrial bipedalism (humans) (Hunt, 1991; Thorpe and Crompton, 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is a statement about hominoid locomotion, with citations to Hunt, 1991 and Thorpe and Crompton, 2006.

claims.claim: Extant hominoid lineages have more significantly diverged in different directions from their last common ancestor with cercopithecoids in terms of positional behavior, which explains why extant hominoids more strongly differ in vestibular features.
claims.source: The fact that, in terms of positional behavior, extant hominoid lineages have more significantly diverged in different directions from their last common ancestor with cercopithecoids explains why extant hominoids more strongly differ in vestibular features—even if the functional link of some vestibular features remains to be better determined.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference about the relationship between locomotor diversity and vestibular morphology variation.

claims.claim: Determining the order in which vestibular features evolved is required to use them for inferring the phylogenetic placement of extinct hominoids.
claims.source: Determining the order in which these features evolved is therefore required to use them for inferring the phylogenetic placement of extinct hominoids.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the methodological requirements for phylogenetic inference.

claims.claim: From the LCA of crown hominoids, great apes and humans appear derived in the opposite direction of hylobatids with regard to their volumetric proportions (stout vs. slender SCs, respectively).
claims.source: From the LCA of crown hominoids, great apes and humans appear derived in the opposite direction of hylobatids with regard to their volumetric proportions (stout vs. slender SCs, respectively).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the ancestral state reconstruction results.

claims.claim: According to the ancestral state reconstruction for crown hominoids, hylobatids appear secondarily convergent with cercopithecoids in terms of SC volumetric proportions.
claims.source: According to our ancestral state reconstruction for crown hominoids, in this regard hylobatids appear secondarily convergent with cercopithecoids.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the ancestral state reconstruction results.

claims.claim: The hypothesis that hylobatids are secondarily convergent with cercopithecoids should be tested by adding extinct stem cercopithecoids and fossil hominoids of less controversial affinities than Oreopithecus to the analysis.
claims.source: However, this hypothesis (and the alternate one, that hylobatids merely reflect more closely the primitive condition for crown catarrhines as a whole) should be tested by means of adding extinct stem cercopithecoids and fossil hominoids of less controversial affinities than Oreopithecus to the analysis.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claims.claim: Hoolock, in agreement with the basal position of this genus among extant hylobatids, apparently retains a more primitive morphology than other hominoids for various features.
claims.source: It is noteworthy that Hoolock, in agreement with the basal position of this genus among extant hylobatids, apparently retains a more primitive morphology than other hominoids for various features.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the morphological analysis and phylogenetic position of Hoolock.

claims.claim: While the characters related to an anteromedial displacement of the lateral SC appear synapomorphic for hominoids, the only incipient vertical compression of the anterior canal SC morphology of Hoolock might be plesiomorphic for hylobatids.
claims.source: While the characters related to an anteromedial displacement of the lateral SC appear synapomorphic for hominoids, the only incipient vertical compression of the anterior canal SC morphology of Hoolock might be plesiomorphic for hylobatids, in which case the marked vertical compression of this canal would be a synapomorphy of hominids only, with the remaining hylobatid genera having also evolved it in parallel.
claims.evidence: The claim is a hypothesis about the evolution of the anterior canal morphology, based on the morphological analysis and ancestral state reconstructions.

claims.claim: Various great ape lineages and humans further diverged from one another from the more derived condition of the reconstructed crown hominoid LCA.
claims.source: While various great ape lineages and humans further diverged from one another from the more derived condition of the reconstructed crown hominoid LCA, as noted above gibbons and siamangs might have secondarily converged to some extent with cercopithecoids by evolving slenderer SCs, presumably as a result of similar evolutionary pressures posed by fast-moving types of locomotion.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the ancestral state reconstruction results.

claims.claim: Gibbons and siamangs might have secondarily converged to some extent with cercopithecoids by evolving slenderer SCs, presumably as a result of similar evolutionary pressures posed by fast-moving types of locomotion.
claims.source: While various great ape lineages and humans further diverged from one another from the more derived condition of the reconstructed crown hominoid LCA, as noted above gibbons and siamangs might have secondarily converged to some extent with cercopithecoids by evolving slenderer SCs, presumably as a result of similar evolutionary pressures posed by fast-moving types of locomotion.
claims.evidence: The claim is a hypothesis about the evolution of hylobatid SC morphology, based on the ancestral state reconstruction results and functional considerations.

claims.claim: Based on the reconstructed ancestral morphotypes, bonobos and (to a lesser extent) chimpanzees would be closer to the LCAs of hominids, hominines, and the Pan-Homo clade, than either humans or the remaining extant great apes (gorillas and orangutans).
claims.source: Based on our reconstructed ancestral morphotypes, bonobos and (to a lesser extent) chimpanzees would be closer to the LCAs of hominids, hominines, and the Pan-Homo clade, than either humans or the remaining extant great apes (gorillas and orangutans).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the ancestral state reconstruction results.

claims.claim: Gorillas and orangutans would have diverged from the hominid LCA in markedly different directions both in terms of SC configuration and stoutness.
claims.source: The latter would have diverged from the hominid LCA in markedly different directions both in terms of SC configuration and stoutness.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the ancestral state reconstruction results.

claims.claim: The results support the view that not only hominins, but also gorillas and, to a large extent, the orangutan lineage diverged from ancestors with a largely Pan-like vestibular morphology.
claims.source: Our results therefore support the view that not only hominins, but also gorillas and, to a large extent, the orangutan lineage diverged from ancestors with a largely Pan-like vestibular morphology.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the ancestral state reconstruction results.

claims.claim: Caution is required when interpreting the pattern of vestibular evolution in locomotor terms, as other selection pressures and/or non-adaptive factors could have potentially played an equally, if not more significant, role in determining vestibular shape variation in hominoids.
claims.source: It would be tempting to interpret this pattern in locomotor terms (e.g., by suggesting a semiterrestrial ancestry not only for hominines, but also for crown hominids as a whole). However, caution is required as other selection pressures and/or non-adaptive factors could have potentially played an equally, if not more significant, role in determining vestibular shape variation in this group.
claims.evidence: This is a cautionary statement about the interpretation of the results.

claims.claim: Australopithecus not only displays the various hominoid synapomorphies mentioned above, but also hominid-like volumetric proportions of the SCs and human-like vestibular features such as large anterior and posterior canals.
claims.source: With regard to the fossil hominoids analyzed here, Australopithecus not only displays the various hominoid synapomorphies mentioned above, but also hominid-like volumetric proportions of the SCs and, as expected in a bipedal hominin, human-like vestibular features such as large anterior and posterior canals.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the morphological analysis of Australopithecus.

claims.claim: The vestibular morphology of Australopithecus is in agreement with the large amount of habitual bipedal behaviors inferred for the almost complete skeleton (StW 573) to which one of the analyzed specimens belongs.
claims.source: This is in agreement with the large amount of habitual bipedal behaviors inferred for the almost complete skeleton (StW 573) to which one of the analyzed specimens belongs (Heaton et al., 2019), as well as previous analyses of the inner ear as a whole (Beaudet et al., 2019b).
